summary: Eielson Air Force Base (EIL/PAEI) is a United States Air Force installation located approximately 26 miles southeast of Fairbanks in interior Alaska. Named after pioneering Alaska aviator Carl Ben Eielson, the base is renowned for its Arctic cold-weather testing capabilities and hosts units equipped with fifth-generation fighter aircraft. The base plays a strategic role in Pacific defense and routinely conducts training operations in some of the harshest flying conditions on Earth.
faqs:
Q: What is Eielson Air Force Base primarily used for?
A: Eielson AFB serves as a key United States Air Force installation hosting fighter wing operations, Arctic warfare training, and cold-weather equipment testing. It has strategic importance for Pacific theater defense.

Q: Can civilians fly into Eielson AFB?
A: Access to military bases is generally restricted to authorized personnel, though the airfield may occasionally support civilian charter or emergency operations. Travelers should coordinate access in advance through official channels.

Q: When is the coldest time to visit Eielson?
A: Winter temperatures in interior Alaska regularly drop below minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit between November and February. Visitors planning travel should prepare for extreme cold and limited daylight.

Q: What is the base named after?
A: The base honors Carl Ben Eielson, an Alaskan bush pilot and aviation pioneer who became the first to fly across the Arctic in 1928 with George Hubert Wilkins.
transport_tips: Travelers heading to Eielson AFB typically fly into Fairbanks International Airport (FAI) and drive approximately 30 to 45 minutes southeast on the Richardson Highway. Rental cars are available at Fairbanks, though winter road conditions can be hazardous and chains or studded tires may be required. Military personnel should confirm gate access requirements before arrival.
local_tip: Layer up seriously; temperatures swing more than 100 degrees between summer and winter at this latitude, and even in milder seasons wind chill off the tarmac can catch visitors unprepared.
